questions.title: Why is there a $1/|y_i|$ exponent in the sequence-level importance ratio $s_i(\theta)$?
questions.question_body: In the definition of GSPO, the sequence-level importance ratio is given as $s_{i}(\theta) = \left( \frac{ \pi_{\theta} (y_i | x) }{ \pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}} (y_i | x)} \right)^{\frac{1}{|y_i|}}$. I understand that $\frac{ \pi_{\theta} (y_i | x) }{ \pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}} (y_i | x)}$ is the standard importance sampling ratio for a sequence. Why is it necessary to take the $|y_i|$-th root? Does this normalization simply keep the value near 1, or does it fundamentally change the gradient $\nabla_{\theta} \mathcal{J}_{\text{GSPO}}$ compared to a standard sequence-level ratio?

questions.title: If rewards are sequence-level, why does the GRPO objective still include a summation over tokens $t$?
questions.question_body: The paper argues that 'the unit of optimization objective should match the unit of reward' and suggests that token-level optimization is problematic because rewards are granted to the entire sequence. However, in Equation 2, the GRPO objective $\mathcal{J}_{\text{GRPO}}$ still contains the term $\frac{1}{|y_i|} \sum_{t=1}^{|y_i|}$. If the optimization is supposed to be sequence-level, why aren't we removing the summation over $t$ entirely, rather than just changing how the importance weight is calculated?

questions.title: How does the $\mathrm{sg}$ operation in GSPO-token maintain numerical identity with GSPO?
questions.question_body: In the GSPO-token variant, the paper defines $s_{i,t}(\theta) = \mathrm{sg} [ s_{i}(\theta) ] \cdot \frac{ \pi_{\theta} (y_{i,t} | x, y_{i,<t}) }{ \mathrm{sg} [ \pi_{\theta} (y_{i,t} | x, y_{i,<t}) ] }$. The authors claim that $s_{i,t}(\theta)$ is numerically equal to $s_{i}(\theta)$. I am confused about how the stop-gradient ($\mathrm{sg}$) operation works here. If we stop the gradient on the denominator, doesn't that mean the ratio $\frac{ \pi_{\theta} (y_{i,t} | x, y_{i,<t}) }{ \mathrm{sg} [ \pi_{\theta} (y_{i,t} | x, y_{i,<t}) ] }$ effectively behaves like a constant during the backward pass? How does this allow the gradient to correctly reflect the log-likelihood of the tokens?

questions.title: Why does 'expert-activation volatility' specifically invalidate importance sampling in MoE models?
questions.question_body: In Section 5.3, the authors explain that in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, the experts activated for a response can change significantly between $\pi_{\theta}$ and $\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}$. They claim this 'invalidates' the importance sampling weight $w_{i,t}(\theta)$. I am struggling to understand the theoretical link here: if $w_{i,t}(\theta)$ is simply the ratio of the probabilities of the tokens, why does the fact that different experts are active in the two models make that ratio mathematically 'invalid' rather than just high-variance?

questions.title: Why does clipping a much larger fraction of tokens in GSPO lead to higher training efficiency?
questions.question_body: Figure 4 shows that GSPO clips a much larger fraction of tokens than GRPO. In most RL settings, clipping more data usually implies we are discarding more of the signal, which should theoretically slow down learning or reduce efficiency. Why does the paper claim this counter-intuitive result is a sign of better efficiency? Is it because the gradients from the non-clipped tokens are significantly more accurate?

questions.title: How does GSPO allow the use of inference engine likelihoods while GRPO does not?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions that GSPO is more tolerant of precision discrepancies between training engines (like Megatron) and inference engines (like vLLM). Why does using a sequence-level likelihood $\pi_{\theta}(y|x)$ solve this problem, while the token-level likelihood $\pi_{\theta}(y_t|x, y_{<t})$ used in GRPO does not? Is it because of the accumulation of floating-point errors over the length of the sequence $|y|$?
